accuracy.evidence: Checked against DfE Development Matters (2021) Physical Development (3-4: comfortable grip with good control; Reception: foundations of a handwriting style that is fast, accurate and efficient), the EYFS 2024 ELG Fine Motor Skills, and Beery VMI norms as summarised in OT pre-writing guidance (vertical line first, then horizontal line and circle around 3, cross around 4, diagonals, square, X and triangle later). Start points and directions follow the National Handwriting Association advice used by UK schemes: lines start at the top or on the left, round letters c, a, o and d start at the top and go anticlockwise. The adult notes say ages vary and the order is a guide, so nothing is stated more firmly than the evidence allows; the 'line down first' rule for a cross is taught as the usual order (the same as the letter t), not as the only correct drawing.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips OT and handwriting guidance names for this age: starting a line at the bottom and pushing up, going across from right to left, starting a circle at the bottom or going clockwise (which later causes a, d and o to be formed wrongly), stopping before the circle joins up, and a cross whose lines meet at an end (T or L). Each one has its own reply in the drawing steps (verdicts back, start, short, wobble, cw, gap, bottom, tee, ell), appears as a wrong drawing by Pip in the right-way step, and has a slip tag in the challenge.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab judges real finger strokes on this topic's own shapes: straight strokes are checked for start point, direction, reaching the end and distance from the guide; circles by unwrapped angle (anticlockwise sweep over 300 degrees), staying on the ring and closing; crosses as two ordered strokes with the across line tested for height (T or L) and direction. Its scenes (rain from a cloud, cars to flags, balls, window crosses, Pip's drawings, a house picture) belong to pre-writing, and the gate measures it under 30% similar to every flagship lab, including flagcaps and flagltrfam, which trace letters.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each rule is discovered by drawing: pushing a rain line up from the puddle gets 'Rain falls down: start at the green dot at the top', a road from the flag gets 'Start on the left, where the car is', a circle to the right gets the c and o reply, a half circle gets 'keep going until you get back to the green dot', and a line across at the top of a window gets 'it makes a T'. Real-drag tests with Playwright confirmed every one of these replies. The right-way step makes the child judge start and direction from someone else's drawing, and the picture step shows the four shapes as parts of things.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: 'At the bottom' for where a line down starts (the cloud and rain make the top obvious once drawn), 'On the right, by the flag' for a line across, 'Round to the right' for a circle (the arrow and the reply for a clockwise stroke), and 'At the top, like T' for where a cross meets (the window only fills when the lines meet in the middle). The done message names what the child predicted.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with answers in rotating positions; every wrong option carries a slip tag with its own message: bottom (starting at the bottom means pushing up), middle (start at the very top), rtl (left to right, the way we read), down (that is a line down, not across or round), cw (c, a, o and d go round to the left), tee and ell (lines meeting at an end make a T or an L) and gap (keep going round until you join up).

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the readability limits (kid at most 6.5, adult at most 9.5). Kid paragraphs are one idea each in very short sentences for ages 3-4 ('A line down starts at the top. Pull it down, like rain falling from a cloud.'). Canvas prompts are one line, steps use concrete things (cloud, puddle, car, flag, ball, window), and button labels are short ('Start at the top', 'Top, round to the left').

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph teaches one shape and its start and direction. Adult paragraphs give the curriculum links and key words, the usual order and the difference between imitating and copying, the named mistakes, and what the lab does. No template text is repeated from other lessons, and the filler gate passes.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at iPhone 13 (390 px) in light and dark and at desktop for every step before and after Show me. Fixes made from screenshots: the rain cloud was drawn from oversized circles that covered the message strip (now a low cloud of small bumps), the two windows touched each other when stacked (smaller windows with a gap), the child's stroke vanished on top of the orange ball (now drawn in dark brown), and the picture step's window and path gaps were under 44 px with tiny question marks (now at least 46-48 px with 22 px marks). The message strip has a fixed height so drawing places never jump; Right way and Wrong way pills are 66 px tall and the lab buttons are 56 px young-size.

accessibility.evidence: Every drawing has button twins that run the same judge, including the wrong ways, with descriptive aria-labels ('Rain line 1: start at the top and go down', 'Ball 2: start at the top and go round to the right', 'Window 1: line across at the top', 'Pip drew a line from the bottom, pushing up: wrong way', 'Put the cross on the window'); the canvas aria-label is updated live with each reply; the challenge uses real buttons and a polite live region; axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes on desktop and phone in the browser gate.
